entry: French colonial territory in mainland North America, 1534–1763. At its 1712 peak, New France comprised five colonies, from Newfoundland to the Canadian Prairies and from Hudson Bay to the Gulf of Mexico. Early activity centered on the [[Fur trade|fur trade]]; successful settlements began in Acadia and [[Quebec]] in the 17th century. The Treaty of Utrecht (1713) ceded French claims in Acadia, Hudson Bay and Newfoundland to Britain. After the [[Seven Years' War]], the 1763 Treaty of Paris ceded the rest of New France to Britain and Spain. Napoleon Bonaparte sold Louisiana to the [[United States]] in the [[Louisiana Purchase]] of 1803.

Second-largest island in the world, in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. The island lies in [[Melanesia]], separated from [[Australia]] by the 150 km Torres Strait; both landmasses sit on the same [[Continental shelf|continental shelf]] and were joined as the landmass of Sahul during low sea levels in the [[Pleistocene]] glaciations. It has the third-largest remaining [[Rainforest|rainforest]] in the world and the highest plant biodiversity of any island. The eastern half is the main landmass of [[Papua New Guinea]], while the western half forms part of Indonesia. The two major cities are [[Port Moresby]] and Jayapura. The Spanish explorer Yñigo Ortiz de Retez named it in 1545, perceiving a resemblance between its peoples and those of the African region of Guinea. Indonesia took control of the west under the 1962 New York Agreement, and a 1969 Act of Free Choice integrated the territory, a process critics have called manipulated.

State in the New England region of the northeastern United States (pop., 2020: 1,377,529). Concord is the capital, and Manchester is the largest city. In 1776 it became the first of the British North American colonies to establish an independent government and state constitution, and its delegates signed the [[United States Declaration of Independence]]. Textile manufacturing and shoemaking drove industrialization after the U.S. Civil War. The state has no [[Income tax|income tax]] or [[Sales tax|sales tax]], relying instead on local property taxes. It is known for holding the first U.S. presidential primary.

City in the U.S. state of [[Connecticut]], on the northern shore of Long Island Sound (pop., 2020: 134,023). [[Yale University]] is the city's biggest employer and taxpayer. New Haven was founded by English [[Puritans]] in 1638, and within a year it was laid out in the Nine Square Plan, one of the first planned cities in the United States. The city was co-capital of Connecticut from 1701 to 1873. It is nicknamed the Elm City after its public tree-planting program, the first in the U.S.

American film movement of the mid-1960s to early 1980s, also called the Hollywood Renaissance. It arose as the [[Studio system|studio system]] weakened after the Paramount Case and the rise of television, and directors such as [[Francis Ford Coppola]] and [[Martin Scorsese]] took a key authorial role. Their narratives often departed from classical norms. Early hits included *Bonnie and Clyde* and *The Graduate* (both 1967), and landmarks included *The Godfather* (1972) and *Taxi Driver* (1976). The movement declined after costly flops such as *Heaven's Gate* (1980), and Hollywood shifted to blockbusters such as *Jaws* and *Star Wars*.

NASA interplanetary probe, launched January 19, 2006. It was the first spacecraft to explore [[Pluto]], flying 12,500 km (7,800 mi) above its surface on July 14, 2015. Built by the [[Johns Hopkins University]] Applied Physics Laboratory, it also flew past [[Jupiter]] in 2007 for a gravity assist and the [[Kuiper belt]] object Arrokoth in 2019. It was the fastest human-made object ever launched from Earth, measured by average speed relative to Earth. As of April 2026 it was 64.45 AU from the [[Sun]]; NASA plans to operate it until it leaves the Kuiper belt, expected in 2028 or 2029.

Period of colonial expansion by the major Western powers and Japan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The participants included the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Russia, the [[United States]] and Japan. The European powers and Japan conquered almost all of [[Africa]] and parts of [[Asia]], motivated by rivalry among the great powers, the economic desire for new resources and markets, and a civilizing mission. The Long Depression of 1873–1896 pressed governments to promote home industry, and Europe's powers abandoned free trade (Germany from 1879, France from 1881). The [[Scramble for Africa]] was formalized at the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885, which defined effective occupation as the basis for recognizing territorial claims, requiring routine armed force against indigenous states. Many colonies gained independence during the era of [[Decolonization|decolonization]] that followed [[World War II]].

U.S. state in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions, the most densely populated in the nation (pop., 2025: over 9.5 million). Its capital is Trenton and its largest city is Newark. Dutch and Swedish colonists made the first European settlements. It was among the [[Thirteen Colonies]], and it hosted several pivotal battles of the [[American Revolution]]. After the [[American Civil War]], it became a major [[Manufacturing|manufacturing]] center and a destination for immigrants. It is known as the Medicine Chest of the World for its biopharmaceutical industry, and strong sectors include [[Finance|finance]], [[Logistics|logistics]] and [[Filmmaking|filmmaking]].

American vocal group from Dorchester, Massachusetts, formed in 1984. Initially conceived as a boy band, it signed with [[Columbia Records]] and sold more than 80 million records worldwide. The members are Donnie Wahlberg, Jordan Knight, Jonathan Knight, Joey McIntyre and Danny Wood. The group won two American Music Awards in 1990 and is often credited with paving the way for later boy bands such as [[Backstreet Boys]] and [[NSYNC]]. It disbanded in 1994 and reunited in 2007 to record an album, then toured in 2008. In 2014 the group received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Period of ancient Egyptian history, 16th–11th century BC, covering the 18th, 19th and 20th dynasties. Egypt reached its greatest territorial extent in this era, after expelling the Hyksos, with campaigns into the [[Levant]] and [[Nubia]]. [[Hatshepsut]] funded a mission to the [[Land of Punt]] and re-established trade networks, and [[Thutmose III]] is recorded as having captured 350 cities. Thutmose I was the first pharaoh to cross the Euphrates. Later reigns included [[Akhenaten]], who attempted a monotheistic reform centered on the Aten, and [[Ramesses II]], whose long reign saw monumental construction. The period weakened under foreign pressure and resource strains, leading to the Third Intermediate Period.

Landlocked state in the Southwestern United States, admitted to the Union on January 6, 1912, as the 47th state. Its capital, Santa Fe, is the oldest state capital in the U.S., founded in 1610 as a seat of government in [[New Spain]]. The 1680 Pueblo Revolt was the first successful revolution against colonial rule in the Americas. After the [[Mexican–American War]], the United States annexed it as part of New Mexico Territory. During World War II, New Mexico hosted key facilities of the [[Manhattan Project]], and the first nuclear test, [[Trinity (nuclear test)|Trinity]], took place there in 1945.

English rock band formed in [[Manchester]] in 1980. Its founders, Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook and Stephen Morris, had been members of [[Joy Division]], which disbanded in 1980 after the suicide of lead singer Ian Curtis. They fused post-punk with [[Electronic dance music|electronic dance music]], and their 1983 single "Blue Monday" became the best-selling 12-inch single of all time. The band was the flagship act of Factory Records and pioneered alternative dance. Hook left in 2007 after personal disputes with the other members. In 2026, the band and Joy Division were inducted as one act into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Consolidated city-parish on the [[Mississippi River]] in [[Louisiana]] (pop., 2020: 383,997). The city is a major port and commercial hub for the Gulf Coast and is known for its music, Creole cuisine and [[Mardi Gras]]. Founded in 1718 by French colonists, it was the territorial capital of French Louisiana before passing to the United States in the [[Louisiana Purchase]] of 1803. It was the largest city in the American South from the Antebellum era until after [[World War II]]. Its historic French Quarter is known for French and Spanish Creole [[Architecture|architecture]]. [[Levee|Levees]] and drainage pumps are meant to protect the city from flooding, but [[Hurricane Katrina]] in 2005 flooded more than 80% of it, killed more than 1,300 people and caused a population decline of over 50%.

State on the east coast of [[Australia]] (pop., 2025: over 8.6 million). Its capital, [[Sydney]], is also the country's largest city, and almost two-thirds of residents live in Greater Sydney. [[James Cook]] claimed the east coast in 1770, and Britain founded a penal colony at Sydney Cove on January 26, 1788. Originally covering more than half of mainland Australia, the colony was divided during the 19th century into what became other states and territories. [[Sydney Harbour Bridge]] (completed 1932) and the [[Sydney Opera House]] (opened 1973) are notable landmarks. Lord Howe Island remains part of the state.

Viceroyalty of the [[Spanish Empire]], 1521–1821, with its capital at [[Mexico City]]. [[Hernán Cortés]] conquered the [[Aztec Empire]] in 1521 and established the capital on the site of [[Tenochtitlan]]. Established as a viceroyalty in 1535, it covered Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and much of the southwestern United States, including California, Texas and Florida, as well as the Philippines and Guam. Silver mining in Zacatecas from the 1540s made it vital to the Spanish crown, and Acapulco was the New World terminus of the trade with [[Manila]]. The [[Mexican War of Independence]] (1810–1821) ended the viceroyalty in 1821.

Second division of the Christian Bible, a collection of 27 texts written in Koine Greek by various authors. It includes four gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, epistles attributed to Paul and other authors, and the [[Book of Revelation]]. Together with the [[Old Testament]], based primarily on the [[Hebrew Bible]], it forms the sacred scripture of Christianity. Its texts recount the teachings and person of [[Jesus]] and events of first-century Christianity. Many texts were written in the mid-to-late first century, though scholars lack consensus on the date of the latest. The canon developed over the first few centuries and was formalized as 27 books by the late fourth century. The earliest manuscripts date from the late second to early third centuries AD, except possibly Papyrus 52. The [[Catholic Church]] and Eastern Orthodoxy regard it as inspired scripture, as do evangelicals and many other Protestants.

Early modern term for most lands in the Western Hemisphere, particularly the Americas and sometimes Oceania. It was introduced in the early 16th century during the [[Age of Discovery]], when Italian explorer [[Amerigo Vespucci]] argued that lands west of the Atlantic were new continents. Before this, European geographers thought the world included only [[Africa]], [[Asia]] and Europe, which were known as the Old World. The [[Columbian exchange]] carried maize, potatoes, tomatoes and tobacco from the Americas to the Old World, and wheat, horses, cattle and pigs in the opposite direction.

Conspiracy theory holding that a secretive power elite plans a totalitarian world government. Adherents allege that a cabal uses front organizations and crises to pursue a globalist agenda that would replace sovereign nation-states. Before the early 1990s it was largely confined to the militantly anti-government right in the United States and to fundamentalist Christians concerned with the [[Antichrist]]. Scholars Michael Barkun and Chip Berlet have warned that it has fueled survivalism and paramilitarism. Woodrow Wilson and Winston Churchill used the phrase in the 20th century for international cooperation, such as the [[League of Nations]] and the [[United Nations]].

Five primate families native to the tropics of [[Mexico]], Central America and South America. Their broad, flat noses, with sideways-facing nostrils, give the parvorder Platyrrhini its name, meaning broad-nosed. Families include marmosets and tamarins, capuchins and squirrel monkeys, night monkeys, titis and sakis, and howler and [[Spider monkey|spider monkeys]]. Monkeys of the family Atelidae, such as the spider monkey, are the only primates with prehensile tails. New World monkeys are thought to descend from African simians that crossed the Atlantic on rafts of vegetation during the [[Eocene]], and the lineage split from other simians about 40 million years ago. Their closest relatives are the [[Old World monkey|Old World monkeys]] and apes. Many species are now threatened by habitat destruction and hunting.

Family of seven living species of vultures and condors, found in the [[Americas]]. They are called New World vultures to distinguish them from [[Old World vulture|Old World vultures]], with which they are not closely related despite similar appearance and behavior. Like other vultures, they are [[Scavenger|scavengers]] with an extremely disease-resistant digestive system and a bald head that helps prevent rotting matter from accumulating while feeding. Some species have a good [[Sense of smell|sense of smell]], whereas Old World vultures find carcasses by sight alone. The family includes the [[Andean condor]] and the California condor, which is critically endangered, with about 560 individuals, including captive birds, as of 2024. The black vulture and turkey vulture are of least concern and expanding northward.

Family of small, often colorful passerine birds restricted to the [[New World]]. They are not closely related to Old World warblers, and most are arboreal insectivores, though the ovenbird and the two waterthrushes are primarily terrestrial. The family likely originated in northern [[Central America]], where the greatest number of species is found, and spread north during interglacial periods, mainly as migrants that returned to the ancestral region in winter. Two genera, Myioborus and Basileuterus, appear to have colonized [[South America]] early, perhaps before the two continents were linked, and together constitute most warbler species there. The family name Parulidae derives from the genus Parula, whose name evolved from the tit genus Parus used by Linnaeus in 1758.

Last day of the [[Gregorian calendar|Gregorian]] year, 31 December, and the evening that marks its end. In many countries it is celebrated with dancing, eating, drinking and fireworks, and many Christians attend a watchnight service. Celebrations generally continue past midnight into New Year's Day, 1 January. The local time zone determines when the new year arrives; the first places to welcome it are the Line Islands (part of [[Kiribati]]), [[Samoa]] and [[Tonga]], west of the [[International Date Line]]. In contrast, [[American Samoa]], Baker Island and Howland Island are among the last to welcome it. In Ghana, fireworks are displayed at midnight across various cities, especially in Accra and Tema. In [[Rwanda]] the president delivers a live end-of-year address at midnight.

[[Rapid transit]] system in [[New York City]], serving [[Manhattan]], Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx. Opened on October 27, 1904, it is one of the world's oldest public transit systems. It has the most stations of any system, with 423 in operation (472 if stations linked by transfers are counted multiple times). It has 665 miles (1,070 km) of revenue track, and 40% of the track is above ground. It is the busiest rapid transit system in the Western Hemisphere by annual ridership, with 2,314,388,000 unlinked passenger trips in 2025. Of its 25 services, 22 pass through Manhattan. It has run 24 hours a day, every day, for most of its history.

American conservative daily tabloid [[Newspaper|newspaper]] published in [[New York City]]. Founded in 1801 by [[Alexander Hamilton]] as the *New-York Evening Post*, a broadsheet. Hamilton's co-investors were [[Federalist Party|Federalists]] dismayed by Thomas Jefferson's election as president. Its best-known 19th-century editor was William Cullen Bryant, under whom it was widely respected. Dorothy Schiff owned it in the mid-20th century; in 1976 [[Rupert Murdoch]]'s News Corp bought it for US$30.5 million. Its coverage has drawn frequent criticism for controversial headlines and accusations of political bias. As of 2026 it is the third-largest U.S. newspaper by print circulation.

American [[Stock exchange|stock exchange]], nicknamed the Big Board, in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan. It is owned by Intercontinental Exchange, an American holding company. Its origins trace to the Buttonwood Agreement, signed on May 17, 1792, by 24 brokers who agreed to give preference to one another in securities sales. The earliest securities traded were mostly government [[Bond (finance)|bonds]], including Revolutionary War bonds. The Civil War greatly stimulated speculative trading, and membership was capped by 1869. Government regulation followed, with the most dramatic changes in the 1930s after a major stock market crash near the beginning of the [[Great Depression]]. It lists more than 2,000 companies, predominantly large firms. In 2012 it imposed rules restricting brokers from voting uninstructed shares.
